name: Gareth Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at an independent garage on the edge of the city, and most of our work is getting used cars ready for the dealer next door. Brakes, tyres, services, cleaning up warning lights so the car passes its check. I've got a diagnosis app on my phone that I use all day, and it's honestly taught me half of what I know. I'm still slow on the big jobs, but I'm quick to find what's wrong.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with a mate from school, and I'm on the low end of pay because I'm still a junior. I sell used parts online in the evenings, wing mirrors, headlights, whatever the dealer's scrapping, and that pays for my phone and food. Savings, maybe two weeks. There aren't many garages round here, and the good ones want five years' experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people overhyped it, simple as that. I'd keep posting my parts listings that AI helps me write. Online I'd probably say the doom crowd got it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me, but it doesn't fix the money. The dealer next door decides how much work we get, and when used car sales drop, we drop. Two weeks of savings is nothing if the dealer has a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the parts selling, maybe add a second platform and do it properly on Sundays. I'd keep using the AI diagnosis app and try to get faster on the spanner side. I'd try to save the parts money instead of spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, my bank account isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the dealer decides your work. How often is it slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every January and every August, pretty much. Last January I did three-day weeks for a month. The parts money I make online saved me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big could the parts selling get?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few hundred a month if I did it properly. Not enough to live on, but enough to stop panicking every January.

say: AI is a **decent tool** that people overhyped.
The **doom crowd** got it wrong, and I'd say so online.
think: The **dealer next door** decides our workload, not AI.
**Two weeks** of savings is nothing if the dealer has a bad month.
do: Grow the **used parts** selling onto a second platform on Sundays.
Keep using the **AI diagnosis app** and get faster with tools.
**Save the parts money** instead of spending it.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a fine job but a weak bank account.
S0.quote: Last January I did three-day weeks for a month. The parts money I make online saved me.
fieldNote: Gareth's work depends on the **used car dealer** next door, which slumps twice a year.
He already has a **side income** selling scrapped parts, written up with AI.
He's an **everyday AI user** who credits the app with much of his learning.

steps.text: List scrapped parts on a second selling platform every Sunday
Use the diagnosis app on every job to get faster
Put the parts money into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but nicely. Mechanics who use the tools will be fine. I'd probably post a few videos showing how I use the diagnosis app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it helps me more than most. The thinking side, finding faults, pricing parts, writing listings, I already do with AI. The risk is the dealer gets software that does the pricing and checks, and needs fewer of us prepping cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new tools come in faster than anyone else at the garage, and offer to train the older lads. I'd start the parts selling as a proper little business. I'd also ask about the high-voltage course, because the used electric cars are coming in now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Slightly nervous about the dealer, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the older lads want you training them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first. Ray, our senior guy, calls my app the toy. But when he sees it find a fault in two minutes that took him an hour, he'll come round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer of us prepping cars. Who goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The slowest on the tools, which right now is me or the other junior. So I'd want to make myself the one who knows the software. Being the one who knows the software is my insurance, because right now I'm the slowest on the tools.

say: Mechanics who use the tools will be fine, so **adapt** or get left behind.
I'd post **videos** showing how I use the diagnosis app.
think: I already do the **thinking side** with AI, so I'm ahead.
Dealer software could mean **fewer of us** prepping cars.
do: Learn new tools **fastest** and offer to train the older mechanics.
Turn parts selling into a **proper small business**.
Ask about the **high-voltage course** for used electric cars.
S1.quote: Being the one who knows the software is my insurance, because right now I'm the slowest on the tools.
fieldNote: Gareth plans to make himself the **software person** to offset weak tool skills.
He sees older colleagues as **converts in waiting**, not obstacles.
His side business would **formalise** under this scenario.

steps.text: Offer to train Ray and the others on new diagnostic tools
Register the parts selling as a small business
Ask the garage about the high-voltage electric vehicle course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and nobody's ready, and we all need to move fast. No point blaming anyone, it's just what's happening. I'd be the guy posting what to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the bit I'm good at, diagnosis with the app, is the bit that goes first in 2028. Then I'm a slow pair of hands until 2031, when robots do tyres and brakes. So I've got about three years where I'm useful, and not much money to play with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the parts business first, because selling stuff online keeps going as long as people have old cars. I'd look for work with whoever services the new robots, even as a trainee. I'd cut my spending right down and save everything over rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, a bit sick. But also a bit, right, let's go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said selling parts keeps going. Does it, if robots fix the cars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yeah. Old cars stick around for years. The robot garages will want cheap parts too, so I'd be selling to them instead of to blokes on driveways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we might need to share a cheaper place, or take a third person. He works in a call centre, so honestly he's worse off than me. I'd tell him to start learning something now.

say: It's **huge** and nobody's ready, so we all need to move fast.
No point **blaming anyone**; it's just what's happening.
think: My **diagnosis skill** goes first in 2028, leaving me slow hands.
Robots do tyres and brakes by **2031**, giving me about three useful years.
do: Go **all in** on the online parts business.
Apply to firms **servicing robots**, even as a trainee.
**Cut spending** right down and save everything over rent.
feel: **Nervous** and a bit sick, but also **ready to go**.
S2.quote: Old cars stick around for years. The robot garages will want cheap parts too, so I'd be selling to them instead of to blokes on driveways.
fieldNote: Gareth reads the **three-year gap** well and plans a bridge through parts selling.
His centre view shows in refusing to **blame anyone**.
He worries more for his **call-centre flatmate** than himself.

steps.text: Expand the online parts business to sell to robot garages
Apply for trainee roles with firms that service robots
Cut spending to rent and essentials only
Move to a cheaper flat or take a third flatmate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, so get learning. I'd share what I'm learning online, courses, tools, all that. Practical stuff, not politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years suits me. Thinking AI in 2031 means my diagnosis edge lasts till then, and robots in 2034 means I'd still have hands-on work for a while after. I could build the parts business and get qualified in something around robots in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the high-voltage course this year and a robotics or electrical maintenance course part-time from year two. I'd try to get the parts business to a few hundred a month. And I'd save a month of rent by the end of year one, which I've never managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but in control. Like I can see the corner coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock the plan over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dealer going bust, mainly. If the garage loses the used car dealer, I'm out before any robot turns up. That's the boring risk nobody talks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to bring along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other junior, Liam, because he's good with his hands and hates screens. If I can get him on the app now, he'll be okay for longer.

say: Five years is a **decent warning**, so get learning.
I'd share **practical** courses and tools online, not politics.
think: My **diagnosis edge** lasts until 2031, and hands-on work a bit beyond.
Five years is time to grow the **parts business** and get qualified.
do: Take the **high-voltage course** this year, then robotics maintenance part-time.
Grow the **parts business** to a few hundred a month.
Save **a month of rent** by the end of year one.
feel: **Nervous but in control**, seeing the corner coming.
S3.quote: If the garage loses the used car dealer, I'm out before any robot turns up.
fieldNote: With five years Gareth builds a **staged plan** of courses, savings and side income.
He names a **boring risk**, the dealer going bust, as bigger than AI.
He'd coach **Liam**, the other junior, on the app.

steps.text: Take the high-voltage course this year
Study robotics maintenance part-time from year two
Grow the parts business to a few hundred a month
Save one month of rent by the end of year one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so no excuses. Learn something, start something. That'd be my whole message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the comfortable one for me. Robots in 2039, I'm thirty-nine, and by then I could have my own small business, maybe mobile diagnostics or parts. The risk is getting lazy because it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get qualified on electric cars, then save for a van with diagnostic kit in about three years. I'd run mobile diagnostics on evenings and weekends before going full time. The parts business would keep going alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. More excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mobile diagnostics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people hate taking cars to garages, and the thinking part I do with the app anyway. A van is cheaper than a building. When the robots come, I'm small enough to pivot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is getting lazy. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set dates. Van by year three, full time by year five. If I miss them, I'll know I'm drifting.

say: Ten years is **loads of time**, so nobody has an excuse to sit still.
Learn something, **start something**: that would be my whole message online.
think: Robots in **2039** give me time to build my own small business.
The real risk is **getting lazy** because it feels far away.
do: Get qualified on **electric cars**, then save for a diagnostics van in three years.
Run **mobile diagnostics** evenings and weekends before going full time.
S4.quote: A van is cheaper than a building. When the robots come, I'm small enough to pivot.
fieldNote: Ten years turns Gareth into a **would-be founder** with dated targets.
He chooses **mobile diagnostics** because it suits his app-based skills and low capital.
He knows his own risk: **drift** when the deadline feels far.

steps.text: Get qualified on electric cars in the first two years
Save for and buy a van with diagnostic kit by year three
Run mobile diagnostics on evenings and weekends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. My best skill goes first and there's not enough money to bridge three years. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small starts, like a van and kit, and short courses that don't need you to quit work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about side hustles. Loads of people my age only stay afloat because of side hustles. When the main job wobbles, the side one keeps the lights on.

headlineQuote: Loads of people my age only stay afloat because of side hustles. When the main job wobbles, the side one keeps the lights on.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** junior who preps used cars for a dealer next door.
He uses a **diagnosis app** all day and sells scrapped parts online in the evenings.
He has about **two weeks** saved, and the dealer's slumps cut his hours twice a year.
He stays **uneasy** in slower scenarios and turns anxious with faster AGI, but always has a plan.
His centre outlook means he **blames no one** and focuses on practical moves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which removes his diagnosis edge with no money to bridge three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** or grants for small starts like a van, plus short **part-time courses**.
